# Is a fresh tyre worth more than the slope says?

The objection this answers: a linear degradation slope has no one-off gain at a stop, so an optimiser built on it should always stop later than a pit wall buying an immediate jump in pace, and pricing that jump in would close the gap in Result 3.

A fit forces its residuals to average zero overall, so the profile is what carries the answer. **Negative means laps faster than the model says.**

The first measured age carries **+0.1867s** — laps on a new set are *slower* than the fit expects, not faster, and the sign only turns over once the set is several laps old. That is tyre warm-up, and it is the opposite of the effect the objection predicts.

Per circuit, fresh laps come in faster than modelled at only **7 of 24** circuits, median **-0.0484s**.

## What this does to Result 3

It makes the gap harder to explain, not easier. The optimiser prices a stop as an instant return to the slope's intercept. Real new tyres need a lap or two to come up to temperature, so the engine is already **over**stating what a stop buys. Correcting it would push the recommended lap later still and widen the disagreement. This is the fourth candidate explanation tested here and the fourth to fail.
